This is achieved by plotting the distributions in opposed directions (as in Figure 5), allowing their curves to intersect. At these intersection points, equivalent values are determined regardless of which scheme is referenced. The mathematical structure underpinning this is an isomorphism between two ordered sets, where the relationship between grades is preserved. For instance, a woman at 96° in her scheme matches a man at 4° in his, indicating a consistent functional mapping. The complementary angle relation further constrains this space: if one scheme’s grade is 20°, its counterpart is 80°. These principles enable robust cross-scheme inference and allow for Bayesian updates of strength likelihoods. Failure modes include non-monotonicity or inconsistent angular offsets, which invalidate the isomorphism. The dual nature of the system also implies a symmetry-breaking mechanism, where the underlying physical properties (e.g., strength) remain invariant under transformation.
